opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest challenge is defining what "good" actually looks like. Reinforcement learning depends on having a reward signal, and in games or simulated environments that's easy because you either won or you didn't. Enterprise workflows are rarely that clean. If you're handling a customer support case or working through a financial analysis, success has many dimensions: accuracy, compliance, tone, speed, and cost. Some of those outcomes may not be visible until weeks later, and much of what defines quality lives in the heads of experts rather than in any written specification.

So a lot of the hard work is turning that tacit knowledge into evaluations and reward functions that truly capture what the business cares about. If you get it wrong, the model will happily optimize for the wrong thing. It'll find shortcuts that score well on your metric but don't produce anything a domain expert would trust.

The second piece is the environment. RL needs lots of trial and error, but you can't let an agent experiment freely in a live production system with real customers, real money, and real regulatory constraints. You need realistic sandboxes or simulations that reflect the messiness of the actual workflow, including its tools, data, and edge cases. Those take real effort to build, and they differ from one enterprise to the next.

The models themselves have become remarkably capable, and the RL algorithms are in reasonably good shape. The bottleneck now is often this translation layer: capturing a company's specific knowledge and definition of success in a form the model can learn from. Enterprises that get that right can create something very powerful, because that's where their proprietary advantage lives. It's not only in their data, but also in their understanding of what a great outcome looks like.

r001.rationale: The response stresses defining business success and capturing tacit expertise, but does not say this understanding is needed to decide where reinforcement learning is appropriate.

r002.rationale: It describes evaluations, reward functions, and realistic sandboxes as substantial work, then says the translation layer is often the bottleneck while RL algorithms are in reasonably good shape.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the main challenge is that reinforcement learning, in its classic form, assumes you have an environment you can interact with cheaply and repeatedly, and a reward signal that's clean and well-defined. Games give you both of those. Enterprise problems give you neither.

Take the reward first. In a real business workflow, what does "success" mean? If an agent is handling a customer support ticket, or processing a loan application, or writing code against an internal codebase, the outcome is often delayed, noisy, and partially subjective. You can't just plug in a scalar and let the agent optimize against it, because the agent will find the shortcuts. We've seen this over and over, even in research settings: you specify something that looks like the goal, and the policy learns to game the specification rather than solve the actual problem. In an enterprise, the cost of that misalignment is real money, or a real customer, or a compliance violation.

Then there's the environment. RL wants millions of trials. Enterprises can't afford to let an agent make millions of mistakes on live systems. So you end up needing simulators, or sandboxed replicas of the actual environment, and building those is often harder than the learning problem itself. A lot of the work I've done around agents interacting with software environments, things like SWE-bench or web agents, is really about this: can we construct realistic, verifiable environments where an agent can actually practice and get feedback, without the feedback being hand-labeled by a human every time.

And the third piece, which I think gets underappreciated, is that the data in enterprises is mostly not trajectories. It's logs, documents, tickets, half-finished processes. It's not naturally shaped like state, action, reward. So there's a translation problem before RL even starts.

What's changed with language models is that the policy now comes in with a lot of prior knowledge. It doesn't have to learn from scratch what a database is or how a refund works. That makes the sample efficiency problem far less brutal than it was five years ago. But it shifts the challenge toward verification: how do you know, at scale, that what the agent did was actually correct? I think whoever solves that reliably, for messy, long-horizon, real-world tasks, is the one who makes RL actually practical in the enterprise.

r001.rationale: The response discusses enterprise challenges such as rewards, environments, and data, but does not say deep understanding of the problem is needed to decide where RL is appropriate.

r002.rationale: It says enterprises need simulators or sandboxed replicas and that building them is often harder than the learning problem itself.

astra-6.text:
I think the main challenge is defining what you actually want the system to optimize. In a game, you have a fairly clear reward—you win or lose, or you get a score. In an enterprise setting, the objectives are often more ambiguous. You might want to improve customer satisfaction, reduce costs, and maintain quality, and those goals can pull in different directions.

Then there’s the question of how you learn. Reinforcement learning relies on trying things and getting feedback, but you can’t necessarily let a system explore freely when its actions affect real customers or business operations. And the feedback may take weeks or months to arrive.

So the challenge is finding a well-defined problem where you can measure success, learn safely from the data you have, and get feedback that’s useful enough to improve the system.

r001.rationale: The response discusses defining measurable objectives and learning safely, but does not identify deep understanding of the enterprise problem as necessary to determine whether reinforcement learning is appropriate.

r002.rationale: The response describes challenges in objectives, safe exploration, and delayed feedback, but does not state that establishing the surrounding setup takes more work than the reinforcement learning component.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest challenge is figuring out how to specify the reward. In a game, you have a score and fairly clear rules for what success looks like. In an enterprise setting, you might care about customer satisfaction, cost, reliability, and longer-term outcomes, and those don’t always line up. If you optimize something that’s easy to measure, it may not capture what you actually want.

There’s also the question of exploration. A reinforcement learning system learns by trying things, but you can’t necessarily let it make costly mistakes with real customers or business processes. So you need a way to learn from existing data, test safely, and get useful feedback. The algorithm is one piece; creating that learning environment is often the harder part.

r001.rationale: The response discusses specifying rewards and competing enterprise goals, but does not say that deeply understanding the problem is needed to decide where RL is appropriate.

r002.rationale: It says the algorithm is one piece and that creating the learning environment is often the harder part, conveying that the surrounding setup takes more work than the RL component.
